newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ risk premium could change conditions mix - BTNZ.
newsitem.headline: NZ risk premium could change conditions mix - BTNZ.

text.p: It could take an increase in the risk premium on New Zealand assets to bring about the mix of higher interest rates and a lower exchange rate that the Reserve Bank has said it would like, Bankers Trust New Zealand Chief Economist David Plank said on Tuesday.
Plank said current account or political concerns could have that effect, but political risk appeared lower this year than last.

Speaking to Reuters at the New Zealand Investment Conference in Auckland, Plank rejected the suggestion that the government might step in to rebalance monetary conditions if present imbalances persisted.
"I don't think the majority party in the coalition believes in it," he said. The conservative National Party leads a coalition with centrist New Zealand First.
Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) governor Don Brash has repeatedly said he would prefer a lower currency and higher interest rates.
Plank was speaking during a break in the conference after an off-the-record speech by Brash and a presentation by Graeme Wheeler of the New Zealand Debt Management Office.

"If the risk premium on New Zealand assets goes up, then you could get a change in the mix," Plank said, adding that higher interest rates would help curb domestic inflation, while a lower exchange rate would help the tradeable sector.
"What may cause investors to change their mind about New Zealand is one, the current account...and the second thing is politics.
"People may get concerned about the direction of politics and so on, but they didn't get that concerned about it last year, and the risks if anything for this year are lower," Plank said.
New Zealand held its first general election under a new proportional voting system in October 1996.
Plank said he did not expect the New Zealand dollar to decline over the next 12 months.

"The view we have is that the New Zealand economy is going to pick up very strongly in the middle of the year and force the Reserve Bank to tighten quite aggressively...I think the Reserve Bank view will be quite different from that."
Plank said it was almost certain that the United States and Britain would move to tighten monetary policy in the next six to 12 months.

"But the view Bankers Trust has is that by the end of this year the Reserve Bank will be forced to tighten by more than offshore, so that the differentials will actually widen. It's unlikely that the Reserve Bank's view is similar to ours just yet," he said.

Asked if he thought the spread between U.S. and New Zealand 10-year maturities' yields was arguably higher than the RBNZ's commitment to price stability would seem to justify, Plank said that over time price expectations in New Zealand, particularly in the household sector, would come down.
That would bring about a decline in the differential between New Zealand and the United States, but could take as long as 20 years.
"It's a very long term thing -- how long does it take to become credible? The Federal Reserve has been doing a good job for 50 years, and Dr Brash has been doing a good job for 10."
